strengths: Clear and relevant problem: adapting decoder-only LLMs into general-purpose embedding models while preserving causal attention and avoiding long prompt/repetition overhead is well motivated for NLP retrieval and representation learning.

The proposed mechanism is simple and practical: a lightweight bidirectional encoder produces a single contextual token, projected into the LLM embedding space, and the final embedding concatenates contextual-token and EOS hidden states. This is easy to understand and plausibly portable across decoder-only backbones.

Empirical coverage is strong. The paper evaluates on full English MTEB across 56 datasets and reports additional MTEB-MINI ablations over 41 datasets, with experiments on S-LLaMA-1.3B, LLaMA-2-7B, and Mistral-7B.

The main results are competitive: Causal2Vec improves over LLM2Vec under the reported public-retrieval-data setting and achieves a top MTEB average among the compared Mistral-7B methods, especially when combined with ICL.

Ablations address the main design choices, including contextual-token use, representation concatenation, bidirectional encoder freezing, token placement, number of contextual tokens, and encoder choice.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported by dataset lists, model names, training hyperparameters, instructions, LoRA settings, and evaluation benchmark details.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. The method is essentially a learned/pseudo-token bridge from an existing bidirectional embedder into an LLM, plus concatenated pooling. This is useful, but not a major algorithmic advance relative to prior prefix/adapter/encoder-LLM bridging ideas.

The empirical gains are often small. On full MTEB, Causal2Vec-Mistral-7B without ICL is only 66.10 versus bge-en-icl few-shot at 66.08, and several ablation gains are below one point. The main-conference case depends heavily on accepting these small average improvements as meaningful.

Fairness of comparison is not fully settled. The paper restricts to public retrieval data, but many baselines are taken from prior reports with differing training recipes, model variants, distillation strategies, and possibly evaluation/instruction details. A fully controlled retraining of the most important baselines would make the claims stronger.

The claimed efficiency advantage is strongest against methods that deliberately lengthen inputs, such as ECHO and bge-en-icl. The method still adds a 110M-parameter bidirectional encoder pass, and the paper does not fully characterize end-to-end memory, batching, indexing throughput, or deployment cost relative to strong encoder-only and bidirectional-LLM alternatives.

The causal-attention mismatch argument is plausible but not conclusively isolated. Results show Causal2Vec beats LLM2Vec in this setup, but the evidence does not prove that bidirectional attention intrinsically harms pretrained semantic extraction rather than reflecting implementation, pooling, training, or data differences.

The role of the bidirectional encoder muddies attribution. Since E5-style encoders are already embedding models, some improvement may come from injecting a pretrained embedding prior rather than from specifically solving causal attention limitations; the BERT/E5 ablation helps but does not fully disentangle this.

Reproducibility would benefit from code, exact preprocessing/sampling scripts, random-seed variance, and clearer reporting of whether all MTEB numbers were generated with the same evaluation package/version and instruction templates. No statistical significance or variance is reported.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence, especially “state-of-the-art” and large efficiency reductions, because they apply under a narrowed comparison set and particular baselines rather than the broader embedding-model landscape.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: adapting decoder-only LLMs into general-purpose text embedding models without changing the causal attention mechanism or adding long demonstrations/input repetitions.

The proposed method is simple and implementable: a bidirectional encoder produces a single contextual token, projected into the LLM embedding space, and the final embedding concatenates contextual-token and EOS hidden states.

The paper evaluates on the full English MTEB benchmark and includes several useful ablations over components, contextual-token count, encoder choice, token placement, and freezing the bidirectional encoder.
The reported efficiency comparison against ECHO and bge-en-icl is a legitimate practical motivation, since those baselines increase sequence length substantially.
weaknesses: The main claims are overextended relative to the evidence. The paper repeatedly argues that bidirectional attention may compromise pretrained semantic knowledge, but this is not directly tested; the evidence is only downstream score comparisons with many confounds.

The empirical gains are often small. On MTEB, Causal2Vec-Mistral-7B improves over bge-en-icl few-shot by only 0.02 average points without ICL, and many task-category wins belong to baselines. The component ablations on MTEB-MINI show average gains of roughly 0.2 to 0.6 points, which are not supported by variance, significance testing, or multiple training seeds.

The fairness of the comparison is not fully convincing. The method relies on E5-base-v2, an already trained embedding model, as a bidirectional encoder, so the claim of training solely on public retrieval datasets is narrower than it sounds. The paper does not sufficiently disentangle gains from the proposed causal-LLM mechanism versus importing capabilities from an existing embedding model.

Several baselines are compared via reported numbers rather than controlled retraining, and the paper does not clearly normalize for backbone, embedding dimensionality, instruction format, hard-negative mining, reranker distillation, or teacher data. This weakens the SOTA framing.

The efficiency claim understates the added cost of running a 110M bidirectional encoder. The comparison emphasizes LLM sequence length and selected datasets, but does not provide a full throughput/memory accounting across the full benchmark or deployment settings.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper provides many hyperparameters and dataset names, but does not specify all implementation details needed to reproduce exact training, hard-negative construction, preprocessing, model selection, evaluation scripts, or whether code/checkpoints will be released.

The analysis of why concatenating the contextual token helps is shallow. Norm plots and pooling ablations do not establish that recency bias is mitigated or that the LLM meaningfully uses the contextual token in the claimed way.

The contribution is incremental: it combines a pretrained sentence encoder, a projection layer, prepended conditioning, and concatenated pooling. These are reasonable engineering choices, but the novelty and conceptual insight are limited for main-conference acceptance.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and practical approach for adapting decoder-only LLMs to embedding tasks: prepend a contextual token produced by a lightweight bidirectional encoder and concatenate contextual/EOS hidden states for the final representation. The method is easy to understand and appears broadly applicable without modifying LLM attention implementations.

The empirical evaluation is broad, using the full English MTEB benchmark across 56 datasets and three LLM backbones. The reported results are strong, with Causal2Vec-Mistral-7B matching or exceeding recent public-data baselines and improving further with ICL.

The ablation suite is useful: the paper studies the contextual token, representation method, bidirectional encoder choice, number of contextual tokens, token position, and freezing/LoRA variants. These experiments support the main design choices rather than relying only on a headline benchmark result.

The efficiency comparison is relevant and persuasive against methods that repeat inputs or add ICL demonstrations, showing large sequence-length and latency reductions relative to ECHO and bge-en-icl few-shot.
The writing is generally clear, and the training/evaluation setup is described with enough detail to make the contribution understandable and likely reproducible in principle.
weaknesses: The central mechanism relies on an existing bidirectional embedding model, especially E5-base-v2, so the framing as improving decoder-only LLMs is somewhat softened: the method is partly a hybrid encoder-decoder embedding system. The paper could more carefully separate gains from the LLM, the added encoder, and prior embedding pretraining in E5.

The main performance gains over strong baselines are modest in several comparisons, often around 0.5-1.3 MTEB average points, and not consistently best across task categories. This makes the main-conference case close rather than unequivocal despite the strong overall result.

Some explanatory claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. In particular, the claim that bidirectional attention modifications compromise pretrained semantic extraction due to attention mismatch is plausible but not directly isolated or tested; the experiments mainly show that this method works well, not that the proposed causal explanation is established.

Fairness of comparisons remains somewhat delicate. Baselines differ in training recipes, use of distillation, synthetic/non-retrieval data, ICL, and architecture changes; although the authors try to restrict to public retrieval data, the paper still depends partly on reported numbers and heterogeneous prior setups.

Reproducibility is decent but incomplete: the paper lists datasets, models, hyperparameters, and instructions, but does not clearly state code/model release, exact preprocessing, hard-negative construction, random seeds, or variance across runs. Given the computational cost, these details matter.

The efficiency analysis is useful but limited to selected datasets and a single hardware setup. A fuller accounting of memory, embedding dimensionality after concatenation, index/storage cost, and the bidirectional encoder overhead would make the practical claims more robust.

Evaluation is centered on English MTEB, despite using multilingual components and some multilingual/Chinese retrieval data in training. Broader language coverage would strengthen the general-purpose embedding claim.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and well-motivated hybrid approach for adapting decoder-only LLMs to embedding tasks: a lightweight bidirectional encoder produces a single contextual token, and the final representation concatenates the contextual-token and EOS hidden states. The mechanism is easy to understand and broadly compatible with causal LLM backbones.

The empirical evaluation is substantial. Results are reported on full English MTEB across 56 datasets and across four decoder-only backbones from 1.3B to 7B parameters, with comparisons to strong recent LLM-based embedding methods under a public-retrieval-data setting.

The ablation section is stronger than average: the authors isolate the contextual token, the concatenation representation, the number and type of bidirectional encoders, token placement, bidirectional vs causal attention, input-noise robustness, and efficiency/sequence-length effects.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported by detailed model names, training datasets, instruction templates, major hyperparameters, LoRA settings, training steps, sequence length, optimizer details, and evaluation subsets. The method itself is not technically complex, which further improves reproducibility prospects.

The efficiency motivation is relevant: compared with methods that repeat inputs or add in-context examples, adding one contextual token can preserve the causal LLM’s sequence length while improving embedding quality.
weaknesses: The main empirical gains are modest relative to the strongest baselines: Causal2Vec-Mistral-7B improves over bge-en-icl by only 0.02 average MTEB points without ICL, and the larger 66.85 result uses an additional ICL strategy. This makes the claimed new state of the art somewhat fragile without statistical testing, multiple seeds, or confidence intervals.

The central framing slightly overstates the method as improving decoder-only LLMs without significant added machinery. The approach depends on an external bidirectional embedding model, E5-base-v2, which is itself a strong pretrained embedder. The paper does not fully disentangle how much of the gain comes from causal-LLM adaptation versus importing representations from an already optimized encoder.

The fairness of the comparison is not completely airtight. The method adds a separate 110M-parameter encoder and doubles the final embedding dimensionality under the default representation, while several baselines may have different dimensionalities, pooling heads, or training recipes. Storage and indexing costs are acknowledged but not evaluated in realistic retrieval settings.

Some claims about generalization to unseen non-retrieval tasks are stronger than the evidence warrants. Training uses public retrieval datasets, some evaluation tasks are retrieval datasets closely related to standard training sources, and the full MTEB average mixes task types. More careful separation of seen-like retrieval tasks from genuinely unseen task categories would make the claim more convincing.

The explanation for why bidirectional attention hurts is plausible but not conclusively established. Figure 3 and Table 15 show performance differences, but the analysis does not rule out implementation choices, pooling changes, training schedules, or backbone-specific effects as causes of the attention-mismatch phenomenon.

Reproducibility would be stronger with an explicit code/model release statement, exact MTEB versioning, exact negative mining/sampling details, and multiple-run variance. Given the small margins over leading baselines, these omissions matter for confidence in the ranking claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: adapting decoder-only LLMs for general-purpose text embeddings without changing the causal attention mask.

The proposed method is simple and technically plausible: a bidirectional encoder produces a contextual token that is inserted into the LLM input, and the final representation concatenates contextual-token and EOS hidden states.

The empirical evaluation covers the full English MTEB benchmark and several decoder-only backbones, with ablations on the contextual token, pooling/concatenation strategy, number of contextual tokens, encoder choice, and inference speed.

The paper provides many implementation details, including model names, training datasets, LoRA settings, batch sizes, sequence length, optimizer settings, and evaluation instructions, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central framing is overstated. The method does not simply improve causal LLM embeddings while preserving the original model; it adds a separately pretrained bidirectional embedding model and an MLP, so the gains may come substantially from ensembling or transferring an already strong encoder rather than solving the causal-attention bottleneck in the LLM itself.

The empirical gains are modest relative to strong baselines: e.g., 66.10 versus 66.08 for bge-en-icl and 65.87 for MGH on MTEB. Without statistical significance, repeated runs, or confidence intervals, the claimed state of the art is fragile.

The comparison is not fully fair on resource dimensions. Causal2Vec uses an additional 110M-parameter encoder and doubles the embedding dimension through concatenation, but the discussion of overhead focuses mostly on LLM sequence length and inference time, not memory, indexing/storage cost, deployment complexity, or latency in realistic retrieval systems.

The ablation against simple embedding concatenation is underdeveloped. A stronger baseline would jointly train comparable fusion mechanisms, normalize dimensions, or compare against using E5-base-v2 directly/ensembled under matched dimensionality and compute. As written, it does not convincingly rule out a generic hybrid-encoder benefit.

Several mechanistic claims are not well supported. Claims about mitigating recency bias rely mainly on a synthetic noise experiment and aggregate MTEB scores; there is little analysis of long-context behavior, position sensitivity, or whether the contextual token is actually used semantically by the LLM rather than acting as another learned feature.

The paper leans heavily on MTEB averages, which can hide task-specific regressions. Causal2Vec is not consistently better across task categories and sometimes underperforms baselines, yet the discussion emphasizes the average score and state-of-the-art framing.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite many hyperparameters: there is no clear code/checkpoint release statement, the exact curated 1.5M training mixture and sampling procedure are delegated to prior work, and some baseline results are imported from different sources rather than rerun in one controlled setup.

The novelty is incremental. The idea of adding an external encoder-derived token to condition a frozen/LoRA-tuned LLM resembles existing multimodal adapter/query-token and representation-fusion designs; the paper does not sufficiently distinguish its conceptual contribution beyond applying this pattern to text embeddings.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically motivated method for decoder-only LLM embeddings: prepend a single contextual token produced by a lightweight bidirectional encoder, then concatenate contextual-token and EOS hidden states. The idea is simple, easy to understand, and targets a real limitation of causal attention for representation learning.

The empirical evaluation is broad and relevant: results are reported on the full English MTEB benchmark across four decoder-only backbones from 1.3B to 7B, with comparisons to both bidirectional-attention and causal-attention LLM embedding methods.

The reported performance is strong. Causal2Vec reaches the best average MTEB score among the compared models trained on public retrieval datasets, and the ICL variant improves further. The method also appears competitive in inference time relative to approaches that repeat inputs or add long in-context examples.

The ablation suite is useful: the paper studies the contextual token, the concatenated representation, number of contextual tokens, choice of bidirectional encoder, token placement, bidirectional vs causal attention, robustness to appended noise, and application to an existing embedding model.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported by detailed training hyperparameters, dataset lists, instructions, model identifiers, evaluation subsets, and compute estimates.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than fundamental. The method relies on an external bidirectional encoder to provide the missing future context, so the claim of improving decoder-only LLMs while preserving the original architecture is partly a framing issue: the LLM architecture is unchanged, but the embedding system is no longer purely decoder-only.

The main numerical gains over strong baselines are relatively small in the no-ICL setting, e.g. 66.10 vs 66.08 over bge-en-icl and 66.10 vs 65.87 over MGH. Without significance estimates, multiple seeds, or confidence intervals, it is hard to judge whether the headline SOTA claim is robust.

The fairness of comparisons is not fully settled. Some baselines are taken from prior work, some use different training strategies or objectives, and the strongest industrial/proprietary systems are excluded for understandable but still limiting reasons. More controlled reruns under the exact same implementation would strengthen the case.

The efficiency claim is plausible but somewhat under-evidenced. The method adds a 110M-parameter encoder and doubles the output embedding dimension, which can matter for indexing and storage. Runtime is reported on selected subsets, but memory, indexing cost, and large-scale retrieval deployment tradeoffs are not comprehensively analyzed.

The central explanation that attention modification harms because of pretrain/fine-tune attention mismatch is suggestive, but not conclusively established. The evidence is mostly empirical correlation across backbones; alternative explanations such as tuning recipe, pooling method, or model-specific implementation details remain possible.

The evaluation is restricted to English MTEB and mostly standard embedding benchmarks. The paper would be stronger with multilingual results, domain-shift experiments, retrieval-index scale tests, or downstream RAG evaluations showing that the embedding improvements matter in practical NLP systems.
Code and model release plans are not clearly stated in the extracted manuscript, which leaves some reproducibility uncertainty despite the useful implementation details.
